reading.title: How a Forecaster Thinks
reading.purpose: See how the steps of analysis turn scattered weather data into a forecast.
paras: Every evening, a weather forecaster faces a puzzle: what will the sky do tomorrow? Nobody can see the future, so the forecaster works the way scientists work, one step at a time. Each step uses a skill that students also practice in class. Following them shows how careful thinking turns scattered facts into a useful prediction.

The first step is to categorize the data. Readings arrive from satellites, radar, weather balloons, and many ground stations, and a forecaster sorts them into groups such as temperature, wind, and moisture. Next, the forecaster must differentiate a harmless cloud from a storm cloud, because the two can look alike from far away. Only measurements, such as how fast the air is rising, can tell them apart.

Then comes the thinking. From a falling pressure reading and a wall of dark cloud, a forecaster can deduce that a storm is moving closer. That is an inference, a conclusion built from clues rather than stated outright. To formulate a forecast, the forecaster writes a clear statement with a time and a place, such as "rain by midnight along the coast." A computer model may then derive a probability by running the same calculation many times with slightly different starting numbers and counting how often rain appears.

A good forecaster also gives a rationale. Why is rain likely? The answer should name the reasons, such as warm, moist air meeting cold air, so that others can check the thinking. Teams then appraise each forecast by comparing it with what really happened and asking how much it can be trusted. If a method keeps matching the weather, it is validated, which means it has been shown to be sound. If it keeps missing, the team changes the method.

Finally, people apply what the forecast says to real decisions. A farmer may delay planting, a pilot may choose a new route, and a family may move a picnic indoors. A forecast is useful not because it is always right, but because it gives people a clear reason to act and a way to learn when it is wrong.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "inference" most nearly means
choices: a measurement taken by a weather instrument
a conclusion reached from clues rather than stated outright
a guess that a person makes without looking at any clues or checking any facts
a prediction that is certain to come true by tomorrow night
qs.why: The sentence defines it: an inference is "a conclusion built from clues rather than stated outright."

qs.q: Which sentence explains why a forecaster states the reasons behind a forecast?
choices: If it keeps missing, the team changes the method.
The answer should name the reasons, such as warm, moist air meeting cold air, so that others can check the thinking.
Teams then appraise each forecast by comparing it with what really happened and asking how much it can be trusted.
qs.why: This sentence says the reasons are named so that other people can check the thinking.

ev.text: The answer should name the reasons, such as warm, moist air meeting cold air, so that others can check the thinking.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Forecasters rely mostly on luck because the weather cannot really be measured at all.
Computers have replaced human scientists in nearly every part of weather forecasting today.
Farmers and pilots are the only people who truly need a weather forecast each day.
Forecasters follow steps of careful thinking to turn data into predictions people can use.
qs.why: Each paragraph adds a step, from sorting data to checking results, and the last explains how people use the forecast.

qs.q: A forecaster sorts readings into temperature, wind, and moisture. Which word from the reading names this step?
qs.why: The reading says a forecaster categorizes the data by sorting readings into groups.
